description: Grupo Aeroméxico, S.A.B. de C.V., through its subsidiaries, provide public air carrier services for passengers and goods. It offers scheduled passenger air carrier services, cargo air carrier services
description_full: Grupo Aeroméxico, S.A.B. de C.V., through its subsidiaries, provide public air carrier services for passengers and goods. It offers scheduled passenger air carrier services, cargo air carrier services, and other services. The company also offers loyalty program management, training, franchise systems, and investment management services. Its network of destinations includes Mexico, the United States, South America, Central America, the Caribbean, Canada, Europe, and Asia. The company was founded in 1934 and is based in Mexico City, Mexico.
ceo_bio: Dr. Andrés  Conesa Labastida Ph.D. | CEO & Director | Age 55
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 16K people. Revenue per employee of $320K ranks in the below the sector median among Industrials peers. Each employee generates $32K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $41 per employee reflects an ownership culture.
financial_summary: Grupo Aeromexico, S.A.B. de C.V is a mid-cap industrials business with a $2.6B market cap on $5.4B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +12% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +4.8pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 39% against a 9% cost of capital — a 30-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 27%.

The business throws off $527M in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.60× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.9× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 2.2× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.5%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.
